analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA from ever enforcing its proposed limits on greenhouse gas emissions from fossil-fuel power plants.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its Senate committee and died when the Congress ended, so the EPA's power plant climate rule faced no legislative block.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the EPA from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing a rule proposed in May 2023 that sets greenhouse gas emission standards and guidelines for new and existing fossil fuel-fired power plants, including the repeal of the prior Affordable Clean Energy rule [S2][S3]. It also would have blocked any substantially similar future rule [S2][S3]. In practice, this would have left carbon pollution from coal- and gas-fired electricity generation without federal limits [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of coal- and gas-fired power plants, and the coal and natural gas suppliers that sell to them, benefit because the rule would have required expensive emission controls, fuel switching, or carbon capture equipment on their plants [S3]. Electricity customers would avoid some compliance costs that utilities might otherwise pass through, at least in the short term [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal- and gas-fired power plant owners

how_it_helps.text: The bill flatly prohibits the EPA from finalizing, implementing, or enforcing the May 2023 proposed rule on greenhouse gas emissions from new, modified, reconstructed, and existing fossil fuel-fired electric generating units [S2][S3].
It also blocks any 'substantially similar' future rule, so the EPA could not simply reissue the standards in a new form [S2].

Supporters argued the rule relied on carbon capture and clean hydrogen technologies that are not commercially proven or cost-effective, and that it would reshape the electricity grid with vast economic consequences [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would bear the cost in the form of unchecked carbon pollution and the associated air quality and climate harms, since power plants are among the largest sources of US greenhouse gas emissions; the bill removes the regulatory check on those emissions [S3]. Communities living near coal- and gas-fired plants would continue to bear local air pollution the broader emission guidelines were meant to address [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel-fired power plants without federal standards, removing the main regulatory lever over one of the nation's largest sources of carbon pollution [S2][S3].
It would strip out the proposed repeal of the Affordable Clean Energy rule as part of blocking the broader rulemaking, locking in weaker standards [S3].

Supporters' strongest argument, stated in the bill's own findings, is that the rule's required technology—carbon capture and clean hydrogen—has not been commercially utilized or shown cost-effective, so the standards could force costly retrofits or plant retirements without a demonstrated path to compliance [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real relief to fossil-fuel generators facing compliance costs, and its sponsors raise a legitimate engineering question about whether carbon capture was ready to be mandated. But the trade it offered was to give up federal control of power plant carbon emissions indefinitely—'substantially similar' rules were barred too—so the public cost was the loss of the primary tool for limiting one of the country's largest emission sources, and the bill's main effect ran against the public rather than for it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Capito introduced the bill on June 12, 2023, with Sen. Daines as cosponsor, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works [S1][S3][S4].
The bill received no further action—no markup, no floor vote—and that referral to the Environment and Public Works Committee was its last recorded action [S5].
It carried only one cosponsor in the Senate, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the EPA retained the ability to move forward with greenhouse gas standards for fossil-fuel power plants, and no congressional prohibition blocked those limits. Power plant operators gained nothing from this bill, while the public kept a regulatory safeguard that the bill would have removed.

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit the EPA from finalizing or enforcing its power plant greenhouse gas rule; it was referred to the committee she sits on and never advanced further.

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; it was the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or any further action, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Sen. Thomas Carper
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or vote, so it never left committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's two supporters were both Republicans, and it drew no Democratic cosponsors; the Democratic-run committee that held it took no action.

industries.note: The bill would have shielded coal plants from the proposed emission standards and guidelines, sparing them costly retrofits or retirement. Its failure leaves them exposed to the EPA rule it aimed to block [S3].

Coal producers in states like West Virginia and Montana would have benefited from weaker power plant emission limits that sustain coal demand; the bill's death keeps pressure on coal consumption intact.
Gas-fired plants were also covered by the proposed performance standards and emission guidelines; the failed bill leaves those standards on the table for them.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and clean hydrogen technology developers
industries.note: The proposed rule treated carbon capture and clean hydrogen as the systems plants would use to comply, which would create demand for those technologies; blocking the rule would have removed that driver, and its failure preserves it [S3].
